cards.q: What problem does Loop Guard solve?
cards.a: Loop Guard protects against a non-designated port incorrectly transitioning to forwarding when expected BPDUs stop arriving (e.g., from a unidirectional link, software failure, or one-way fiber issue), which could create a Layer-2 loop.

cards.q: What state does Loop Guard place a port in, and how does it recover?
cards.a: Loop Guard places the port in a loop-inconsistent state (blocking) when expected BPDUs are lost. It recovers (returns to normal STP) automatically once valid BPDUs are received again.

cards.q: On which types of ports does Loop Guard act?
cards.a: Loop Guard acts on non-designated ports (Root, Alternate, or Backup) and is especially useful where expected BPDUs could stop arriving. It should not be enabled on edge/PortFast ports.

cards.q: Why should Loop Guard not be used on PortFast/edge ports?
cards.a: Because an edge port does not expect regular BPDUs to keep frames flowing; Loop Guard is for non-designated STP ports where BPDU loss indicates a failure.

cards.q: How does Loop Guard differ from UDLD?
cards.a: UDLD detects unidirectional links at the physical/link level (one direction working, one not) and can error-disable a port. Loop Guard works at the STP layer by detecting the loss of expected BPDUs on a non-designated port.

cards.q: What command enables Loop Guard on an interface and globally?
cards.a: spanning-tree guard loop per interface and spanning-tree loopguard default globally.

cards.q: Which Cisco STP protection triggers on the loss of BPDUs and creates a loop-inconsistent state?
What is the key difference between Root Guard and Loop Guard behavior?
cards.a: Root Guard reacts to a superior BPDU (root-inconsistent, blocking). Loop Guard reacts to missing expected BPDUs (loop-inconsistent, blocking).

cards.q: Does Loop Guard error-disable or permanently shut down the port?
cards.a: No. It blocks (loop-inconsistent) and can automatically recover, unlike an err-disable.

cards.q: Why might Loop Guard be used together with UDLD?
cards.a: Because they address related failure modes (unidirectional link and lost BPDUs) but Loop Guard is STP-layer and UDLD is link-layer; designers often use them together for redundancy.

cards.q: Which commands verify loop-inconsistent state and Loop Guard status?
cards.a: show spanning-tree inconsistentports shows blocked/inconsistent ports; show spanning-tree vlan 10 / show spanning-tree interface Gi0/1 shows state; show spanning-tree summary can show loopguard; log messages confirm.

cards.q: What is the mental model for Loop Guard?
cards.a: If a non-designated port stops receiving expected BPDUs, block it (loop-inconsistent) instead of risking an accidental forwarding loop.

cards.q: How do Root Guard, BPDU Guard, and Loop Guard compare?
cards.a: Root Guard: blocks on superior BPDU (root-inconsistent). BPDU Guard: err-disables edge port on unexpected BPDU. Loop Guard: blocks non-designated port on lost BPDUs (loop-inconsistent). All protect different aspects of the spanning tree.

cards.q: What is the key concept of Loop Guard in one sentence?
cards.a: Loop Guard prevents an accidental Layer-2 loop by blocking a non-designated port that loses expected BPDUs, using the loop-inconsistent state.

cards.q: Why is it wrong to say Loop Guard is for access/edge ports?
cards.a: Loop Guard is for non-designated ports where BPDUs are expected; edge/PortFast ports normally do not use it.

cards.q: Why is it wrong to say Loop Guard error-disables the port?
cards.a: It places the port in loop-inconsistent (blocking) state, not an error-disable.
